name: Test Coverage Conventions
description: This module governs the naming, structure, and style conventions expected when working on test coverage so output stays consistent and easy to review.
content:
This module governs the naming, structure, and style conventions expected when working on test coverage so output stays consistent and easy to review.

CORE GUIDELINES
1. Before starting test coverage work, confirm the scope and constraints so the approach matches the actual requirement.
2. Keep test coverage changes scoped to what was asked; avoid unrelated cleanup in the same pass.
3. When test coverage guidance conflicts with a specific user instruction, defer to the user's explicit instruction and note the conflict.
4. When test coverage decisions are ambiguous, favor the option that is easiest to reverse or extend later.
5. When multiple test coverage strategies are viable, name the trade-off explicitly rather than silently picking one.
6. Check that test coverage terminology is used consistently throughout, matching existing conventions in the surrounding context.
7. Validate test coverage outputs against a concrete example before treating the work as complete.
8. Surface known limitations of a chosen test coverage approach instead of presenting it as complete when it is not.
9. State assumptions about test coverage explicitly before proceeding, rather than leaving them implicit.
10. Re-check edge cases relevant to test coverage (empty input, boundary values, concurrent access) before calling the task done.
11. Prefer the simplest test coverage approach that satisfies the requirement over a more general one that isn't needed yet.
12. Keep test coverage outputs reproducible: fix seeds, record versions, and avoid hidden non-determinism where it matters.

COMMON PITFALLS TO AVOID
- Avoid mixing unrelated test coverage concerns into a single change; keep each change focused.
- Do not silently drop test coverage edge cases to make an example look cleaner than the real system.
- Avoid introducing new test coverage abstractions before there is a second concrete use case that needs them.
- Do not apply generic test coverage advice without checking it fits the specific context at hand.
- Do not skip documenting test coverage assumptions just because they seem obvious in the moment.

CLOSING NOTE
These guidelines are a starting point for test coverage, not an exhaustive rulebook — use judgment when a rule doesn't fit the situation.
